name: Indexing Conventions
description: This module governs the naming, structure, and style conventions expected when working on indexing so output stays consistent and easy to review.
content:
This module governs the naming, structure, and style conventions expected when working on indexing so output stays consistent and easy to review.

CORE GUIDELINES
1. When indexing decisions are ambiguous, favor the option that is easiest to reverse or extend later.
2. Check that indexing terminology is used consistently throughout, matching existing conventions in the surrounding context.
3. Keep indexing outputs reproducible: fix seeds, record versions, and avoid hidden non-determinism where it matters.
4. Prefer the simplest indexing approach that satisfies the requirement over a more general one that isn't needed yet.
5. When indexing guidance conflicts with a specific user instruction, defer to the user's explicit instruction and note the conflict.
6. Keep indexing changes scoped to what was asked; avoid unrelated cleanup in the same pass.
7. Measure before optimizing any indexing bottleneck; do not guess at what is slow.
8. Document any non-obvious indexing decision with a short rationale so future readers understand the 'why', not just the 'what'.
9. When multiple indexing strategies are viable, name the trade-off explicitly rather than silently picking one.
10. Re-check edge cases relevant to indexing (empty input, boundary values, concurrent access) before calling the task done.
11. Prefer explicit, readable indexing solutions over clever ones that are hard to verify.

COMMON PITFALLS TO AVOID
- Avoid mixing unrelated indexing concerns into a single change; keep each change focused.
- Avoid introducing new indexing abstractions before there is a second concrete use case that needs them.
- Do not treat a single passing example as full verification of indexing correctness.
- Do not silently drop indexing edge cases to make an example look cleaner than the real system.
- Do not skip documenting indexing assumptions just because they seem obvious in the moment.

CLOSING NOTE
These guidelines are a starting point for indexing, not an exhaustive rulebook — use judgment when a rule doesn't fit the situation.
